questions.q: How does a Restriction Rule differ fundamentally from OWD, sharing rules, teams, and Apex managed sharing?
options: It only applies to custom objects, never standard objects
It removes visibility to matching records for matching users, starting from whatever access they'd otherwise have
It grants additional access on top of the baseline, just like the other mechanisms
It requires Modify All Data for every user it applies to
questions.explain: Every other mechanism in the chapter is additive — it grants access on top of a baseline. A Restriction Rule is the one declarative tool that takes access away from a subset of otherwise-visible records.

questions.q: What two components make up a Restriction Rule?
options: A Territory Type and a Territory Model
An AccessLevel and a RowCause
A sharing set profile and an access mapping
User criteria (who the rule applies to) and record criteria (which records get hidden from them)
questions.explain: A Restriction Rule matches on both user criteria and record criteria simultaneously — only where both match does the record disappear from that user's visibility.

questions.q: A Developer Edition org already has two Restriction Rules on the Account object and needs to hide a third distinct category of records from a different user group. What must the architect do?
options: Create the third rule on a different object and use a lookup to simulate the restriction
Switch the org-wide default to Private instead
Consolidate the new requirement into one of the existing rules' combined criteria, since Developer Edition caps at two Restriction Rules per object
Nothing — Restriction Rules per object are unlimited in every edition
questions.explain: Restriction Rules are capped per object by edition — two per object in Enterprise and Developer Edition, five in Performance and Unlimited — so additional exception categories typically must be consolidated into existing rules' criteria.

questions.q: A rep has broad sharing access to every Lead in the system, but a Scoping Rule limits their default Lead list view to their own territory. What happens if that rep runs a report with 'Filter by scope' turned off?
options: The Scoping Rule automatically disables itself for that report
The report can return Leads outside their territory, because their underlying sharing access was never changed by the Scoping Rule
The report fails with a permissions error
The report still only returns Leads in their territory, since the Scoping Rule overrides all reports
questions.explain: A Scoping Rule only narrows the default record set shown by default — it never changes actual sharing access, so disabling scope filtering reveals the rep's full underlying access.

questions.q: A requirement states: 'This user must never be able to see legally restricted records, no matter how they try to query them.' Which tool satisfies this, and which tool would fail to?
options: Neither tool can satisfy this requirement — only lowering OWD can
A Scoping Rule satisfies it; a Restriction Rule would fail to
Both tools satisfy this requirement equally
A Restriction Rule satisfies it, since it changes actual access; a Scoping Rule would fail to, since it only changes default views
questions.explain: A Restriction Rule changes real, underlying visibility, so it holds regardless of how the user queries. A Scoping Rule only changes what's shown by default and can be bypassed by turning off scope filtering or writing an unscoped SOQL query.
